meta.blurb: Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert ask for a boy to help on their farm, and a talkative, red-haired girl arrives instead. Anne Shirley fills Green Gables with imagination, mistakes and love. Will the lonely orphan finally find a home, a best friend and a place to belong?
meta.bible: Anne Shirley: an eleven-year-old orphan with red hair, a huge imagination and a quick temper; she spells her name with an e. Matthew Cuthbert: an old, shy, gentle farmer who loves Anne at once. Marilla Cuthbert: his sister, stern, practical and kind underneath. Mrs Rachel Lynde: the nosy, outspoken neighbour. Diana Barry: Anne's best friend, her bosom friend, dark-haired and kind. Mrs Barry: Diana's mother, who is strict. Minnie May: Diana's little sister, who has croup. Gilbert Blythe: a clever, handsome schoolboy who teases Anne about her red hair and later becomes her friend. Mr Phillips: the first teacher at Avonlea school. Miss Stacy: the inspiring new teacher. Josie Pye: a girl at school, spiteful and proud. Mrs Spencer: the woman who brought Anne to Bright River. Mr Allan: the minister at Avonlea. Mrs Allan: his wife, loved by Anne. Mr Barry: Diana's father, who rents Green Gables land. Green Gables: the Cuthberts' farmhouse. Avonlea: the village on Prince Edward Island. Bright River: the railway station. White Way of Delight: Anne's name for the apple-tree road. Lake of Shining Waters: Anne's name for Barry's Pond. Queen's Academy: the teachers' college in Charlottetown. Charlottetown: the island's main town. Redmond: the college Anne could attend. Carmody: a nearby village with a school. Prince Edward Island: Canada. Hopetown: where the orphan asylum was. Author: L. M. Montgomery, 1908. Voice and tone: warm, funny and affectionate, full of nature and imagination; sad moments, including Matthew's death, are stated gently and plainly; the ending is hopeful.

A1A2: Matthew and Marilla wanted a boy to help on their farm.
Matthew drove to the station to meet the orphan boy.
But a little red-haired girl was waiting there, and her name was Anne.
Anne talked all the way home, and she loved the white apple trees.
Marilla was surprised, because she and Matthew wanted a boy, not a girl.
Anne told Marilla that she had no parents and had worked in many homes.
Marilla meant to send Anne away, but in the end she kept her.
A neighbour, Mrs Lynde, called Anne plain, and Anne lost her temper.
Marilla told Anne to say sorry, and Anne did it loudly.
On Sunday, Anne went to church in a hat full of flowers.
Marilla taught Anne her prayers and her work, and Anne learned fast.
Anne met Diana, a kind girl, and they promised to be best friends.
Marilla lost a pretty pin, and Anne said she took it, but she did not.
Marilla found the pin in her scarf and said sorry to Anne.
At school, a boy called Gilbert called Anne Carrots, and she hit him.
Anne would not speak to Gilbert, and they began a long contest at school.
Anne gave Diana a red drink, but it was wine, and Diana felt ill.
Diana's mother said the girls could not play together, and Anne cried.
Diana's little sister was very sick, and Anne saved her life.
Anne baked a cake for a visitor, but she used the wrong thing.
A new teacher, Miss Stacy, made lessons fun, and Anne loved school.
Anne climbed onto a roof for a dare, fell and hurt her foot.
At Christmas, Matthew gave Anne a beautiful dress with big sleeves.
Anne and her friends wrote stories and read them to each other.
Anne tried to make her red hair black, but it turned green.
Marilla cut off Anne's green hair, and Anne learned a lesson.
Anne lay in a small boat on the pond, but the boat began to sink.
Gilbert came in a boat and saved Anne, but she did not thank him.
Anne spoke at a concert in the hall, and everyone clapped.
Miss Stacy taught a special class, and Anne studied hard for the college test.
Matthew's heart was weak, and the doctor said he must not worry.
Anne and Gilbert took the test in town, and they got the same top mark.
Anne spoke at a hotel concert, wearing a white dress.
Anne went to the college in town and worked very hard all year.
Gilbert won a gold medal, and Anne won a prize to go to university.
Anne came home, and Matthew said he loved her more than ten boys.
Matthew had put his money in a bank, and the bank was failing.
Matthew read the bad news in the paper and died suddenly at home.
Many people came to Matthew's funeral, and Anne cried for a long time.
That night Marilla held Anne and said she loved her like a daughter.
Marilla's eyes were getting worse, and she thought she must sell the farm.
Anne decided not to go to university, because she wanted to stay with Marilla.
Anne planned to teach, and a neighbour agreed to rent the farm fields.
Mrs Lynde told Anne that Gilbert had given up his job for her.
Anne thanked Gilbert, and the two became good friends at last.
Anne began teaching the village children and she enjoyed her work.
Marilla's eyes did not get worse, and Anne read to her every evening.
Anne and Diana stayed best friends and often talked about the future.
Anne visited Matthew's grave and promised that she would make him proud.
Anne walked home in the evening light and felt hopeful about her life.
B1B2: Mrs Rachel Lynde, the nosiest woman in Avonlea, sees Matthew Cuthbert driving off in his best clothes and goes to ask Marilla why. She learns that the Cuthberts, who are getting old, have asked an orphanage for a boy to help on their farm.

Matthew drives to the station at Bright River, feeling nervous because he is shy with everyone, and especially with women. He expects a boy, but he finds only a small, red-haired girl sitting patiently on a pile of shingles.

The girl is Anne Shirley, eleven years old, and she tells Matthew that she is not afraid because she imagined he would come. Matthew is far too shy to tell her about the mistake, and he decides to take her home and let his sister explain.

On the drive home, Anne talks without stopping about everything she sees, and she gives names to places that please her. She calls the road of apple trees the White Way of Delight, and the pond the Lake of Shining Waters.

Marilla is astonished to see a girl in the kitchen, and she tells Matthew that a boy was wanted. Anne understands that nobody wants her, and she bursts into tears, because she has dreamed of a real home.
The next morning, Marilla asks Anne to tell her story. Anne explains that her parents died when she was a baby, and that she has since worked in other people's homes, minding children.

Marilla means to send Anne back to the orphanage, but she sees how fond Matthew has become of the girl. After some careful thinking, she decides to keep her, although she warns Anne that she must be good.

Mrs Lynde comes to meet Anne and says honestly that she is very plain, with freckles and hair as red as carrots. Anne is so furious that she stamps her foot and tells Mrs Lynde she is rude, fat and unkind.
Marilla is shocked by the quarrel and makes Anne apologise at once. Anne goes to Mrs Lynde and kneels on the floor with great drama, and Mrs Lynde is so amused that she forgives her.

On Sunday, Anne decides to wear a hat, but she has none, so she makes one from wild roses and buttercups. Marilla is cross, but the church is delighted by the strange, bright hat and the happy girl beneath it.
Marilla teaches Anne her prayers and how to do small jobs around the house. Anne is eager but often forgetful, because her mind is always full of stories and dreams.

Anne meets Diana Barry, a kind, dark-haired girl who lives nearby, and they like each other at once. They swear a solemn promise in the garden to be best friends for ever, and Anne has never been so happy.

One day Marilla's beautiful amethyst brooch goes missing, and she is sure that Anne has taken it. Anne says she did not, but when Marilla forbids her to go to a picnic, she confesses to a lie so that she can go.

After the picnic, Marilla finds her brooch tangled in the fringe of her shawl, and she realises she has accused Anne wrongly. She says she is sorry, and Anne forgives her at once with a warm and generous heart.

At school, a handsome boy named Gilbert Blythe tries to get Anne's attention by pulling her braid and calling her Carrots. Anne is so angry that she cracks her slate over his head, and the teacher makes her stand in front of the class.
Anne refuses to speak to Gilbert, even when he later says he is sorry. From then on the two compete to be top of the class, and neither of them wants to be the first to give in.
Anne invites Diana to tea, and she brings out what she thinks is raspberry drink. It is really a bottle of currant wine, and Diana becomes very dizzy and has to be helped home.
Mrs Barry is angry and decides that Anne is a bad influence, so she forbids Diana to play with her. Anne weeps as if her heart will break, and even Marilla feels sorry for her.

One night Diana's little sister, Minnie May, becomes seriously ill with croup, and nobody is at home to help. Anne, who has looked after many children, saves the child's life, and Mrs Barry thanks her sincerely.

Anne decides to bake a cake for the minister's wife, but she makes a terrible mistake. She uses a bottle of medicine instead of vanilla, and the cake tastes so strange that the visitor can hardly swallow it.
A new teacher, Miss Stacy, arrives at the school, and she is lively and clever. Her lessons are full of stories and outdoor walks, and Anne decides that she loves her teacher more than anyone.
One day Anne's friends dare her to walk along the roof of the farmhouse. She tries it and falls, and although she is only hurt, she learns that dares are rarely worth the risk.
Matthew sees that the other girls wear dresses with puffed sleeves, while Anne's clothes are plain. He is shy, but he goes to a shop and buys her a beautiful dress as a Christmas gift.
Anne and her friends form a story club, where each girl writes a tale and reads it out. Anne's tales are full of ladies and tragedies, and Diana and the others are charmed.
A salesman visits the house, and Anne buys a bottle of dye, hoping to turn her red hair black. It turns it a dreadful green instead, and she is ashamed to leave the house.

Marilla can do nothing but cut off all Anne's hair, and Anne looks in the mirror and cries. She learns that being good matters more than being pretty, and in time her hair grows back, a darker auburn.
Anne decides to act out the story of the Lily Maid and lies down in a small boat on the pond. The boat has a leak and begins to fill with water, and she grips a pole of the bridge to save herself.
Gilbert Blythe happens to be rowing past and pulls Anne safely into his boat. She is cross and embarrassed, so she refuses to thank him or forgive him for the earlier insult.
The pupils hold a concert in the hall, and Anne is asked to recite a poem. She is terrified at first, but she stands up bravely and the audience cheers.

Miss Stacy forms a class to prepare for the entrance examination to Queen's Academy, where pupils train to become teachers. Anne joins, and she works harder than ever, because she wants to be able to look after Marilla.
Matthew has often felt ill, and one day the doctor tells him that his heart is weak. He must avoid strong feeling and heavy work, but the old farmer does not complain, and Anne is proud of him.
Anne and the other students travel to Charlottetown to take the exam. When the results come in, Anne and Gilbert have the same top mark, and the whole village celebrates.
That summer, Anne recites at a concert at the grand hotel in White Sands, wearing a white dress. The audience claps for a long time, and she has never felt so proud.
Anne goes to Queen's Academy, where she stays in town and works long hours, because she wants to finish the course in a year. She makes new friends, but she often thinks of Green Gables.
At the end of the year, Gilbert wins the gold medal, and Anne wins the scholarship that will take her to Redmond College. She rushes home to tell Matthew and Marilla the happy news.
Anne arrives at Green Gables, taller and more grown up, and Matthew looks at her with pride. He tells her quietly that he would rather have her than a dozen boys, and she is deeply moved.
Matthew's savings are in the Abbey Bank, and a rumour is going round that it is about to fail. When he reads the news in the paper, he is badly shocked, and Marilla sees that he looks very pale.
Matthew goes to his door, and there he dies quietly of a heart attack, and Anne is the first to reach him. The farm falls silent, and Anne cannot believe that her kind friend has gone.
The whole village comes to Matthew's funeral, and many people say kind things about him. Anne cries for hours, and then she feels guilty because she was able to laugh for a moment during the day.
That night Marilla, who has never been good at showing her feelings, finally speaks. She tells Anne that she loves her like her own child, and that she has been the joy of her life.
Marilla's eyes are failing, and the doctor says she must stop reading or she may go blind. With Matthew gone, she thinks she will have to sell Green Gables, and her sadness is plain to see.
Anne lies awake that night and thinks hard about what she owes Marilla. In the morning she tells her that she has decided to give up the scholarship and stay at home.
Anne explains that she will teach at a nearby school, and Mr Barry will rent the farm fields for a fair price. Marilla is deeply touched, and her eyes fill with tears of gratitude.
Soon afterwards, Mrs Lynde calls on Anne with surprising news. Gilbert Blythe has given up the Avonlea school so that Anne can teach it, and he will teach in another village instead.
Anne meets Gilbert on the road and thanks him sincerely, and she asks him to forgive her for being so stubborn. He says there is nothing to forgive, and the two decide to be friends.
Anne begins to teach at Avonlea school, and she soon grows fond of her pupils. She is kind and patient, and she remembers how it felt to be a lonely child.
Marilla's eyesight stops getting worse, and she is able to read a little with strong glasses. In the evenings Anne reads aloud to her, and the house is full of warmth.
Anne and Diana remain close friends, and they often walk together in the autumn woods. They talk about their hopes for the future, and Anne is sure that their friendship will last.
One evening Anne goes to Matthew's grave and places white roses on it. She promises quietly that she will always try to be a good daughter, and that she will never forget his kindness.
Anne walks home in the golden light and thinks about the bend in the road ahead. She does not know what is around it, but she is sure that it holds good things, and she is no longer afraid.
C1C2: Mrs Rachel Lynde, who prides herself on knowing everybody's business in Avonlea, notices Matthew Cuthbert driving away in his best suit and cannot rest until she has found out why. Marilla receives her visit calmly and explains that she and Matthew, who are no longer young, have decided to adopt a boy from an orphan asylum to help with the farm work. The neighbour shakes her head over the scheme, convinced that nothing good will come of such a reckless plan.

Matthew, who is so bashful that he would rather face a charging bull than speak to a stranger, sets out for the railway station at Bright River, hoping to meet the boy as quietly as he can. As the buggy rattles along the quiet country road beneath the bright spring sky, he rehearses the few words he will need. Little does he imagine that the child waiting for him will turn his whole quiet life upside down.

At the empty station, instead of the sturdy boy he expected, Matthew finds a thin little girl with two long red braids and a shabby bag, who seems perfectly at ease. She announces that she is Anne Shirley, that she had been sure he would come for her, and that she has been imagining all sorts of delightful things. Too shy to explain the mistake, Matthew decides that it can wait until they reach home and that his sister will know what to do.

All along the road to Green Gables, Anne chatters without pause, astonished and delighted by every blossoming cherry tree and every glimpse of pond or hill. She names the tunnel of white apple blossoms the White Way of Delight and the shining pond the Lake of Shining Waters, since the plain names seem to her far too poor for such beauty. Matthew, who has never heard so many words from anyone in his life, discovers with surprise that he does not mind in the least.

In the farmhouse kitchen, Marilla stares in blank astonishment at the child who has come in her brother's company, and the truth comes out at once. Anne, understanding that no one wants her after all, bursts into passionate tears, and the sight of her despair unsettles even the stern woman. It seems that the girl who has dreamed of a home all her life is about to be sent away from the first one she has seen.

The next morning, Marilla questions her visitor and listens while Anne pours out the story of a life that has been far from easy. Her parents died when she was a baby, and since then she has been passed from one household to another, minding other people's children and never knowing what it is to be loved. Marilla, who has never been fond of sentiment, finds herself more moved than she is willing to admit.

Marilla's first intention is to send the girl back to the asylum, but the days that follow slowly change her mind. She sees how Matthew has taken to the strange child with quiet and shy affection, and she begins to suspect that she herself is not as hard of heart as she imagined. At last she announces that Anne may stay, though she warns her sternly that she will be expected to behave.

Mrs Lynde calls to inspect the new arrival, and she declares, with the honesty on which she prides herself, that the girl is dreadfully thin, plain and freckled, with hair like carrots. Anne, who has never learned to hide her feelings, flies into a fury, stamps her foot, and tells the visitor she is a rude and unkind woman. Marilla is mortified by the outburst, while Mrs Lynde is secretly more amused than offended.

Determined that her ward shall learn manners, Marilla orders her to go to Mrs Lynde and make a full apology. Anne obeys, but with such a flood of dramatic words and such an elaborate display of remorse that the old lady cannot help laughing and forgives her at once. Marilla, who has been trying to hide a smile of her own, begins to see that bringing up this child will never be dull.

On the first Sunday, Anne, having no hat suited to her taste, trims one with wild roses and buttercups, and sets off for church with her chin held high. The congregation stares at the odd, colourful decoration, but the girl beneath it is so happy that most people are charmed rather than shocked. Marilla, who is horrified by such a display, finds that she cannot bring herself to scold the radiant child.

Marilla begins to teach Anne her prayers, her chores and her manners, and she is surprised by the speed with which the girl learns. Anne is eager and affectionate, but her dreamy mind often wanders, and the kitchen frequently suffers from her forgetfulness. Slowly, however, the old house begins to feel like a place where a child belongs.

Anne soon meets Diana Barry, the dark-haired, rosy-cheeked daughter of the neighbouring farm, and the two girls recognise one another at once as kindred spirits. In the garden, beside a quiet fence, they swear a solemn vow to remain faithful friends for ever, and Anne has never in her life been so happy. She is certain that nothing in the world, however great, could ever part them.

One day, Marilla's treasured amethyst brooch goes missing, and she is convinced that Anne has borrowed it without leave. Anne denies it, but when she is forbidden from going to a long-awaited picnic, she invents a confession so that she may attend, saying that she lost the jewel in the pond. Marilla is furious, and Anne, who has told her first lie, is more miserable than ever.

After the picnic, Marilla discovers her brooch, caught in the fringe of her own shawl, and she is overcome with shame at having doubted the child. She goes to Anne's room and begs her pardon, admitting plainly that she was in the wrong, and that she should have trusted her. Anne, who has already forgotten her own grief, flings her arms around her guardian's neck.

At school, a handsome, laughing boy named Gilbert Blythe tries to win the attention of the new girl by tugging at her braid and calling her Carrots in front of the whole class. Furious, Anne hits him on the head with her slate so hard that it breaks, and the teacher, Mr Phillips, makes her stand in front of the room. She will never forgive him, she resolves, no matter what he says in the years to come.

From that day, Anne will not so much as glance at Gilbert, even when he sincerely apologises and holds out a friendly hand. Yet the more she snubs him, the more eager he becomes to please her, and the two fall into a fierce contest for the highest marks in the school. Neither will yield an inch, and the other pupils watch the rivalry with great interest.

Anne, who longs to play the perfect hostess, invites Diana to tea in Marilla's absence and proudly serves her a bottle of what she believes to be raspberry cordial. It is in fact a strong currant wine, and Diana, after several glasses, becomes dizzy and has to be helped home. Anne has no idea what she has done, and she is deeply wounded by the sorrows that follow.

Mrs Barry, outraged by what she believes is Anne's wickedness, forbids her daughter to play with the girl ever again. Anne is heartbroken, and she weeps with such abandon that even Marilla, who thinks the punishment a little unfair, cannot help feeling sorry for her. Days pass, and the Green Gables kitchen is gloomier than it has ever been.

One night, Diana's little sister, Minnie May, falls seriously ill with the croup, and neither parent is at home to help her. Anne, who has nursed three sets of twins in her earlier life, runs to the house, uses what she knows, and saves the child's life before the doctor arrives. Mrs Barry, humbled and grateful, begs her pardon, and Anne is welcomed back into the family with open arms.

Anxious to impress the minister's wife, who is coming to tea, Anne bakes her first great layer cake and hopes that it will be perfect. In her excitement, she mistakes a bottle of medicine for the bottle of vanilla, and the cake emerges so oddly flavoured that the guest can hardly swallow a mouthful. Anne is ashamed, but Mrs Allan is so gracious that the matter ends in laughter.

When a new teacher, Miss Stacy, takes charge of the school, Anne finds that she has at last met someone who understands her imagination. The lessons become lively and full of stories, and the pupils are taken out in the fields to study nature at first hand. Anne decides that she would follow her new teacher anywhere and begins to dream of a future as a teacher herself.

One afternoon, Anne's friends dare her to walk along the high ridge of the roof, and, too proud to refuse, she climbs up and takes a few steps before she loses her balance. She slides to the ground and sprains her ankle, a punishment that she bears with unusual humility. From that day she vows never again to accept a foolish dare, however much it wounds her pride.

Matthew, who has noticed that the other girls wear fashionable dresses with puffed sleeves while Anne's clothes remain plain and dull, makes up his mind to do something about it. With enormous shyness, he walks into a shop in the village, and after a long and awkward conversation, he comes away with the finest dress he can afford. On Christmas morning, Anne opens the parcel, lifts out the dress with its enormous, shining sleeves, and weeps for sheer joy.

Anne and her friends, eager to make something worthy of their talents, organise a story club in which each girl composes a tale and reads it aloud to the others. Anne's stories are always full of ladies in distress, noble knights and tragic deaths, and her friends listen spellbound. In time, though, Miss Stacy teaches her that simplicity and truth make better stories than exaggeration.

Desperate to be rid of her red hair, Anne buys a bottle of dye from a travelling peddler and applies it with enthusiasm, expecting to see a glossy black. To her horror, her hair turns a dull and dreadful green, and she cannot bear to be seen by anyone. For several days she hides in her room in humiliation, and the whole village is soon aware of the disaster.

There is nothing left to do but to cut the ruined hair as short as possible, and Marilla performs the task gently while Anne weeps. The girl looks at her cropped head in the mirror and learns, bitterly, that vanity brings its own penalty. Marilla, however, consoles her by saying that her hair will grow, and that kindness of heart is far more important than looks.

Inspired by the poem about the Lady of Shalott, Anne, Diana and their friends decide to act out the story, with Anne as the lily maid floating down the river in a boat. She lies down in the old flat boat, and the pond carries her away, but the boat springs a leak and begins to sink beneath her. In terror, she manages to cling to a bridge pile and wait for rescue.

Gilbert Blythe, who happens to be passing in his own boat, hears her cries and pulls her safely aboard, quite at a loss to understand how she came to be in such a plight. Anne, drenched, humiliated and furious, thanks him stiffly and refuses his offer of friendship once again. Deep in her heart she suspects that she is being foolish, but her pride is not yet ready to give way.

At the school concert held in the village hall, Anne is asked to recite, and she stands up at the front of the crowded room, her heart hammering in her chest. Her voice trembles at first, but as she begins to speak, the words flow freely, and the audience listens in silence and then bursts into loud applause. Matthew, who sits at the back, beams with pride, and Marilla, who is too stern to show her feelings, wipes her eyes.

Miss Stacy forms a special class of her older pupils to prepare for the entrance examination of Queen's Academy, where young people train to become teachers. Anne joins at once and begins to study with all the energy she can muster, for she dreams of earning a living and repaying her guardians. Gilbert is in the class too, and their old rivalry takes on a new and more serious tone.

Matthew, who has been working harder than a man of his age should, grows weak, and one day he is struck by a sudden pain in his chest. The doctor examines him and warns that his heart is far from sound, and that he must avoid strain and any shock to his feelings. The old farmer takes the news without complaint, though Marilla and Anne begin to worry quietly.

Anne and her classmates travel by train to Charlottetown for the entrance examination, and for several days she works in a fever of nerves. When the pass list is published, she and Gilbert are found at the very top, tied for first place, and the village rejoices in the success of its young scholars. Anne, to her own surprise, finds that she is glad to share the honour with him.

That summer, at a concert at the great hotel in White Sands, Anne is asked to recite before an audience of wealthy visitors, and she wears a white dress to mark the occasion. Her performance is so moving that the audience applauds for a long time, and she feels, for the first time, that she belongs among people of the world. Yet she looks forward to returning home, because no hotel, however splendid, can compare with Green Gables.

In the autumn, Anne goes to Queen's Academy in Charlottetown, where she makes new friends, works long hours and resolves to finish the two-year course in a single year. Though the city is exciting, she often thinks of the quiet farm, of Matthew's shy smile and of Marilla's firm voice. She studies with extraordinary determination, and neither the cold of winter nor the loneliness of the town can discourage her.

At the end of the year, the results are announced, and Gilbert wins the gold medal, while Anne wins the Avery scholarship, which will pay for her to attend Redmond College. She hurries home on the train, her heart full of pride and happiness, eager to tell the two people who have made it all possible. Even in her triumph, however, she is already planning how she will repay them.

When Anne arrives at Green Gables, she is taller and prettier, and Matthew, who watches her come through the gate, feels a surge of love and pride. He tells her quietly that he would not trade her for a dozen boys, a declaration that moves her more than any speech of praise. Marilla, hiding her own emotion, tells him that he is a foolish old man, but her eyes are shining.

Matthew has placed all his savings in the Abbey Bank, and one afternoon a rumour reaches the farm that the bank is about to fail. He reads the news in the paper and turns pale, and Marilla, noticing his face, urges him to rest. Anne, looking after him, is worried, but she cannot know that the shock will prove too great for his weakened heart.

As Matthew stands by the door of the house, he sways, and before Anne can reach him, he falls to the ground, never to rise again. The doctor is summoned, but there is nothing that anyone can do, and the old man has passed away quietly of heart failure. Anne cannot weep at first, for the loss seems so great that it has stunned her into silence.

The funeral is held two days later, and the whole village gathers to pay respect to the gentle old man who had been so loved by his neighbours. Anne weeps by the grave for hours, and later she is troubled by guilt when she finds herself laughing at a happy memory. Mrs Lynde gently tells her that Matthew would not have wished her to grieve for ever.

That night Marilla, who has never been able to speak of her feelings, sits down beside Anne and, with great difficulty, tells her that she has always loved her as her own daughter. She admits that she was stern and rarely showed affection, but she says that Anne has been the joy of her life. The two sit together and weep, and the old house is quiet around them.

Soon afterwards, Marilla's failing eyesight becomes a serious matter, and the doctor warns her that she may go blind if she does not stop reading and sewing. With Matthew gone, she believes that she has no choice but to sell Green Gables, and she tells Anne about her decision with a heavy heart. Anne listens in silence, aware that the choice before her will change the whole course of her own life as well.

That night Anne lies awake for hours, weighing the future that lies before her against the debt she owes to Marilla. By morning she has made up her mind, and she announces that she will give up the scholarship, because no university can be worth the loss of a home. She says that she will stay and teach, so that the house need not be sold.

Anne explains that she has arranged to teach at a school in the nearby village of Carmody, and that Mr Barry has agreed to rent the farm's fields at a fair price. Marilla, who had never dreamed of such devotion, is overcome with gratitude, and she says that her sacrifice is more than she can ever repay. Anne simply replies that the farm is her home, and that nothing in the world would persuade her to leave it.

A few days later, Mrs Lynde calls to give Anne some unexpected news: Gilbert Blythe has given up his position at the Avonlea school so that Anne may teach there instead. He has taken the post at Carmody himself, in order that she might stay close to Marilla. Anne is silent for a moment, astonished that the boy she has avoided for so many years should have done her such a kindness.

On her way home, Anne meets Gilbert on the road, and for the first time in years she looks him in the face and thanks him warmly. She tells him that she is sorry for her stubbornness all those years, and that she would be glad to count him among her friends. He smiles, takes her hand, and the old quarrel is forgotten in an instant.

Anne opens her school in the autumn, and she soon grows fond of the children, whom she treats with the kindness and understanding she remembers needing herself. She teaches them to love stories and nature, and she is never too busy to listen to a child's troubles. The village, which once thought her an odd little orphan, now holds her in great esteem.

To everyone's relief, Marilla's eyesight stops declining, and with the help of strong glasses, she is able to read a little in the evenings. Anne reads aloud to her whenever she can, and the old house, once so quiet, fills with the sound of stories and gentle talk. Marilla, who has never learned to say what she feels, shows her gratitude with an extra helping of pudding.

Anne and Diana, now young women, still spend their afternoons walking together through the autumn woods, talking over their hopes and their secrets. They agree that, whatever happens, nothing will ever break the vow they swore beside the garden fence so many years ago. Anne feels that she has been truly blessed with a friend who is as faithful as the seasons.

One quiet evening, Anne walks to the small churchyard where Matthew lies and places a bunch of white roses on his grave. She whispers that she will always try to be worthy of his love, and that she will never forget the shy, gentle man who first brought her home. The wind stirs in the trees, and it seems to her that he has heard.

As the sun sets, Anne walks home along the road to Green Gables, and she reflects that her path has taken a turn she had not foreseen. She does not know what lies beyond the bend, but she believes that there will be good things waiting there, and that she can meet them with courage. With Marilla at home and a friend like Gilbert beside her, she has learned that there is more to life than ambition, and her heart is full of hope.
